Across 34 cases from 1996 to 2026, the highest-value exits did the same six things in roughly the same order; Punctual Pros is about 30 months into its own version. First, the sponsor put an operator team in charge at entry: Alpine named Apex's CEO and CFO on launch day in July 2019 with $100M+ of committed equity, American Capital gave Service Experts' returning CEO about 10% ownership, and Huron recruited Sciens' CEO before it bought its first company. Second, the first add-on came early and close to home, a median of about 7 months after entry across 11 dated cases, as Smith + Howard did with Market Street Partners in month 9 and Punctual Pros did with Horvath in month 8.
Third, the tuck-ins kept coming at roughly one every three to five months: Trivest did 16 at TurnPoint while revenue grew nearly 10x, Huron did 13 at Sciens while revenue and EBITDA rose more than 35x, and BSP did nine at Smith + Howard while headcount went from about 100 to about 800. Fourth, every brand ran on one system: CenterOak ran a single IT system and consolidated purchasing at Service Champions, Wrench now books online at 99% of its locations on ServiceTitan, and Authority Brands moved Punctual Pros and every other One Hour, Benjamin Franklin and Mister Sparky location onto ServiceTitan in September 2024. Fifth, they built recurring revenue that buyers pay for: Champions grew from about 60,000 members in 2021 to about 150,000 in 2026 (about 71 to 83 per technician) and sold to Blackstone in February 2026 at a reported ~18.5x trailing EBITDA, while Frontdoor gets 76% of its revenue from renewals with 84% of customers on auto-pay.
Sixth, they owned the technician pipeline: Champions more than doubled its field technicians from 850 to 1,800+, Shermco grew certified technicians from 400+ to 600+ as Gryphon doubled revenue and sold for about $1.6B, and Sila bought a trade school in January 2026. Margin beat volume in the best compounders, as VWR grew Adjusted EBITDA 8.6% a year against 3.7% sales growth from 2006 to 2013 and IES grew operating income 88% on 21% more revenue in FY2024. In the last 12-18 months before a sale the winners kept buying and published KPIs: Shermco closed five add-ons in the 17 months before Blackstone, Sila added four brands in the nine months before Goldman's ~$1.7B (~17x) purchase, and Smith + Howard disclosed more than 600 employees and ~$175M of expected revenue about five months before TPG signed.
Most exits went to a larger sponsor, often with the seller or management rolling equity (Charlesbank into GI Partners at ARS, Odyssey alongside Blackstone at Champions, BV alongside BSP at Frontline), and the median first-sponsor hold was about 4.4 years (4.0 in residential home services). The failures show what not to copy: Any Hour signed 16 partnerships in about 13 months and its loan now carries PIK (payment in kind: interest added to the loan instead of paid in cash) at ~89% of par, TurnPoint grew from 17 to 65 brands and now pays PIK under a new CEO, Horizon is lender-supported, and Roto-Rooter's parent Chemed raised ad spend about $11M from 2023 to 2025 while segment revenue fell about $50M. For Punctual Pros the order is an integration leader and a ServiceTitan KPI pack now, members per technician as the north-star metric, one contiguous tuck-in per quarter in PA, NJ, MD and DE, a Lancaster academy with Thaddeus Stevens, leverage near the 2.9-3.3x lower-middle-market norm, and an exit-ready KPI pack by about 2028.

How each criterion is scored

Sector essentiality (non-discretionary demand) · 15%
Share of revenue tied to repair, replace, compliance, regulated or mission-critical outsourced work. Measure from service-line mix on the website, NAICS code and customer type, and for residential services the repair-vs-install mix and Google review volume.
5>80% non-discretionary (repair, compliance, managed services)
350-80%
1<50% or discretionary consumer product

Company-level: Punctual Pros, Frontline and CET are non-discretionary (repair, managed services, electrical and wastewater service) = 5; Thomas Scientific lab supply is repeat but proved cyclical after the COVID peak = 3.

Fragmentation and add-on runway · 15%
Count of owner-operated firms in the sub-sector within 150 miles of the company (ZoomInfo/Census CBP establishments; add-on target lists). BSP pace is 1-2.4 add-ons per company-year, so the target is 10+ actionable candidates.
5>=25 independent targets in footprint
310-24
1<10

Counted live: independent, non-sponsor targets in the company’s own screen. 25 or more = 5, 10–24 = 3, under 10 = 1.

Recurring or repeat revenue and contract visibility · 12%
Percent contracted or recurring revenue (Frontline 92-93% on 3-5 year contracts); membership/maintenance-plan penetration for home services; repeat audit/tax clients for CPA firms; consumables share for distribution. Sources: CEO interviews, FDD Item 19, service-agreement counts on the website.
5>=85% recurring
340-85%
1<40% project/one-off

Not in the target screens. Held at a neutral 3 until diligence measures contracted or membership revenue.

Founder or management transition readiness, with a CEO who will stay · 10%
Founder or family owner with long tenure who wants a partner rather than a full exit (rollover appetite). For a secondary, an identified CEO-succession bench. Signals: founder age and tenure, generation (Horton is third-generation), named second-tier leaders, a sell-side adviser engaged.
5Founder staying 3-5 years and leading M&A, plus a successor identified
3Founder staying, thin bench
1Owner exiting fully, no successor

Ownership class (founder or family with 20+ years = 4, founder or family or franchisee = 3.5, independent = 3, unverified = 2, sponsor-owned, subsidiary or ESOP = 1), averaged with the screen’s own ownership-readiness sub-score. A 5 needs proof the owner stays with a successor named, which only a first call can supply.

Thematic tailwind that BSP research has already identified · 10%
The target sits inside a theme BSP has publicly named (outsourcing and workforce virtualization; energy capacity and critical infrastructure; legal-IT outsourcing and cyber; housing-stock and weather-driven home services; transatlantic policy complexity). Evidence: a public BSP quote or strategy-page sector list plus a measurable driver (permits, deeds, regulation, rate cases).
5Named BSP theme plus a measurable driver
3Adjacent to a named theme
1No theme

Proxy: rank inside the company’s own screen (fit score encodes the company thesis). Top fifth = 5, then 4, 3, 2, bottom fifth = 1, so companies with different screens compare fairly.

Size band (entry and add-on) · 8%
Portfolio company: est. EBITDA $2-20M core (observed estimates from ~$2-3M at Punctual Pros to $16-20M at Frontline; Thomas at $40-55M was the outlier), equity check $8-90M with SPV (a fund vehicle set up for one deal) co-invest above ~$40M. Add-on: $1-5M EBITDA or 10-150 employees (Frontline's stated tuck-in ~$5M revenue / $1-2M EBITDA). Estimate via PPP payroll, headcount x revenue-per-employee and Form D amounts.
5Portfolio company $3-20M EBITDA / add-on $1-5M
3Portfolio company $2-3M or $20-40M
1<$2M or >$40M

Add-on band of 10–150 employees = 5; 5–9 or 151–250 = 3; otherwise 1. Without headcount, modeled revenue of $3–40M = 4, else 2. Unknown = 2.

Geographic adjacency, with a regional champion that can go national · 8%
Straight-line miles to the nearest portfolio company node (<=60 mi best). Regional share in the home market; one new adjacent state or metro per year.
5<=60 mi or fills a named gap
360-150 mi
1>150 mi with no node

Straight-line miles to the nearest portfolio company hub (Punctual Pros: Lancaster, Harrisburg, York, Toms River; CET: Worcester, Taunton, Norwell, Horton CT). 60 mi or less = 5, 60–150 = 3, beyond = 1. Frontline and Thomas Scientific use the screen’s geography sub-score (fills a named gap = 5). CET targets in New York score 1.

Downside protection: earnings quality, cyclicality and leverage · 8%
Normalize for one-off peaks (Thomas COVID testing: federal revenue fell from $84-91M to $7-8M a year; BPI election-cycle billings). Leverage <=5x at entry with a DDTL for add-ons. Customer concentration <10%. Watch BDC (business development company: a listed private-credit fund that reports its loans) marks after close.

3Some cyclicality
1Peak-cycle earnings or >6x

Risk flags: start at 4 (a 5 needs earnings, leverage and concentration data from diligence), minus 1 per serious flag (union model, acquirer or anti-sale stance, sponsor or ESOP owner, concentration, regulatory), minus 0.5 per business-risk flag (key-person, cyclical or seasonal demand, contested market, non-core revenue) and per data-gap flag. Size and distance flags are not counted twice. Thomas Scientific targets lose 1 more because the company loan is marked near 88% of par.

Tech-enablement / AI upside · 7%
Gap between current tooling and best practice: field-service software, CRM, AI service desk, offshore delivery. S+H's exit cited AI and an India delivery center; Frontline launched the HELIX AI service desk; BPI has ChangeOS. Check job posts, vendor case studies and web stack.

11 points behind the estimates

Pre-deal scale: CET's April 2020 PPP loan ($2.062M, 121 jobs) implies about $9.9M of annual payroll. At the 30–40% labor-to-revenue ratio typical of commercial electrical contractors, 2019 revenue was roughly $25–33M.
By October 2025 CET reported about 140 employees (the brief's ~160 'licensed professionals' may count differently). Applying $250–375k revenue per employee, bracketed by IES Holdings' ~$328k, gives 2025 standalone revenue of about $35–55M (midpoint ~$45M).
At the 8–12% EBITDA margins seen at Limbach (~10%) and IES (~13%, high end), CET's standalone EBITDA at entry was probably about $3–6M, a true lower-middle-market company.
The equity structure supports that scale. The only co-invest was one LP writing $7.5M (Form D, first sale Feb 5, 2025), from a ~$335M fund where a typical position is $25–50M. Total equity was therefore likely ~$25–45M.
Applying the brief's 3.5–5.5x LMM leverage to $3–6M of EBITDA implies $10–33M of senior debt at close. Entry enterprise value was likely ~$35–75M (~9–12x), but none of the debt is visible.
No BDC (business development company: a listed private-credit fund that reports its loans) schedule, lender press release, Form D debt vehicle or credit rating names CET, 'CET Acquisition Holdings, LLC' or Horton. EDGAR full-text search found zero hits and 73 downloaded BDC/credit-fund filings were negative. So the facility most likely sits with a bank or a non-SEC-reporting private lender or SBIC.
BSP's March 2026 Form ADV marks the CET co-invest vehicle at $8.504M against $7.5M invested (1.13x gross). That modest markup fits the NuWave tuck-in plus organic growth, not a re-rating.
NuWave was tiny at acquisition (PPP: 4 jobs in 2020, founded 2019) and adds engineering/design-build capability, not scale; call it $2–10M of revenue (low confidence).
Horton is the transformational add-on. Its 2020 PPP ($646k, 42 jobs, ~$3.1M payroll) has grown to 120+ staff, so revenue is plausibly ~$25–40M today. CET says the deal 'nearly doubles' the workforce.
Pro forma for the first two add-ons (before the October 2026 deals), the company was roughly 260–290 employees, $65–100M revenue and $6–11M EBITDA (low confidence); the company site now states 400+ professionals after four further add-ons reported in October 2026, and these estimates are not restated. Horton was bought by the CET LLC subsidiary with no new BSP Form D, so it was likely funded with incremental or delayed-draw debt (credit the company draws later, as add-ons close) plus seller rollover, pushing leverage toward the upper half of the 3.5–5.5x band.
Offsetting positives: a clean OSHA history, no material litigation, full PPP forgiveness, and state-funded program work (MassCEC On-Street Charging prime vendor, CT Clean Water Fund wastewater exposure via Horton). Watch items: a likely related-party lease of Horton's Canton facility (97 River Road CBP, LLC) and a possible Duquette-affiliated mechanical firm (A. Duquette & Son) across the street from CET HQ.

What the record does not show
8 gaps

SEC/BDC: EDGAR full-text search (2019–2026) returned 0 hits for 'Commonwealth Electrical Technologies', 'Commonwealth Electrical', 'CET Acquisition Holdings', 'Horton Electrical' and 'NuWave Energy'. 73 locally cached BDC/credit-fund 10-K/10-Q/N-CSR filings (ARCC, GSBD, BCRED, ASIF, OHA, MFIC, etc.) also had no match. No BDC loan line, lender 8-K or lender press release found, so the debt facility, agent, pricing and maturity are unknown.
Credit ratings / private-credit press: no KBRA/Moody's/S&P/Fitch or 9fin/Debtwire/PE Hub debt reference found. The PE Hub NuWave article is paywalled.
MA entity details (CET Inc. conversion/merger, CET Acquisition Holdings formation) and MA UCC-1 secured parties (agent bank) are not captured.
The MassCEC On-Street Charging contract value is not published.
Prevailing-wage and public-works award records naming CET or Horton with contract values were not found. No CT municipal WPCA bid tabulations or CT DEEP Clean Water Fund contractor awards were located.
CourtListener: complaint amounts in the SunEdison adversary proceeding are unavailable (documents not in RECAP).
NuWave's PPP record has anomalous use-of-proceeds fields (payroll blank, mortgage interest $125,680), so NuWave payroll cannot be derived.
The relationship of A. Duquette & Son, Inc. and of the Devens mailing address on CET's OSHA records to CET is unverified.

How the score works

CET fit index (0–100). Counties are scored on commercial establishment density, healthcare and manufacturing establishment counts, 90-day commercial permit volume and value, a data-center proxy score and an EV-infrastructure score, then indexed to the top county (Middlesex MA ≈ 98.5). Tiers: Tier 1 ≥ 60, Tier 2 50–60, Tier 3 below 50. The original model did not publish its weights, so read scores as relative. CT counties have no population, establishment or permit inputs (a data gap, not a lack of demand). Thesis first, essential services, founders stay
Twelve observations

BSP buys theme-first: each deal release frames the company as the output of a sector thesis studied in advance, from RJ David's 'over a year' in electrical services before CET to Adam Glucksman's watch on accounting before Smith + Howard.
Since 2024 the filter has narrowed to essential services. Punctual Pros, Frontline and CET are all non-discretionary, and Fair Harbor remains the only discretionary consumer bet and the only portfolio company besides Frontline with no add-ons.
Anchor acquisitions come from two kinds of seller: sponsor secondaries for the larger checks (Thomas from Carlyle, BPI from Svoboda, Frontline from BV) and founder or partner owners taking first institutional capital for the smaller ones (Fair Harbor, Smith + Howard, Punctual Pros, CET).
In secondaries the outgoing sponsor often rolls a minority (Svoboda at BPI, BV at Frontline), and the inherited CEO is replaced at about 13-15 months (Simmons to Haas at Thomas, Naidoo to Britt at Frontline) while founder CEOs such as Sean Taylor, Matt Buckwalter and John Duquette Jr. stay.
Anchor acquisitions are bought in banked processes (6 of 7 had a named sell-side adviser, and Punctual Pros went to 'eight finalists'). Berenson advised BSP on Thomas, BPI, Frontline and CET, Harris Williams on Punctual Pros and Frontline, and Morrison Cohen or Greenberg Traurig was counsel on every deal.
The first add-on typically closes 6-9 months after the anchor acquisition (NCI at 6.1 months, BOLDT 7.6, Horvath 8.0, NuWave 8.0, Market Street 9.0), and the median is 8.0 months.
Add-ons are small founder-, family- or partner-owned firms (Day Associates with 10 people, Smith Kesler with 30+, Horton with 120+). None of the 21 identified came from a PE seller, and many were sourced through relationships, such as Matt Buckwalter's decade-long tie to Horvath.
Add-ons alternate between filling in geography (Market Street, Smith Kesler, Horton Lee & Burnett, Horvath, Horton) and adding new capabilities that create cross-sell (VIP, Fahrenheit, Geels Norton, Message House, Agado, NuWave).
Each company is financed with a private-credit unitranche (a single term loan that blends senior and junior debt) from a different direct lender (Apollo/MidCap at Thomas, PineBridge at BPI, PGIM at Punctual Pros, NXT and Audax at Frontline), with delayed-draw (credit the company draws later, as add-ons close) or amendment capacity sized for the add-on program.
Larger companies get a deal-named co-invest SPV (BSP-TS, BSP-BPI Holdings, BSP-FL, BSP-CET). Against a $335M Fund I, a company needing more than about $40M of equity depends on co-investors such as Carlyle AlpInvest.
Smith + Howard is the template so far: about 100 professionals grew to about 800 through 9 add-ons and a tech, AI and offshore build-out, and the firm was sold to TPG Growth after 3.7 years with William Blair and Baird running the process.
Thomas Scientific shows the value of leaving room in the debt for add-ons and a refinancing. For the next deals the implied rubric favors $3-20M EBITDA essential-services leaders in fragmented regional markets with a founder CEO who will stay and run M&A, a warm first add-on, and a credible tech-enablement story.

Home sales in the footprint (Punctual Pros). Reading now: 8,270 homes under contract. −8.8% vs a year ago. Today: Hurts. High. What to do: Mail every buyer within 60 days of closing. New movers. Size (est.): Today's −8.8% ≈ −$70.3K sales a year est.

Mortgage rates (Punctual Pros). Reading now: 7.28%. +1.02 pts vs a year ago. Today: Hurts. High. What to do: Lean on repair-first offers and monthly financing. New movers.

Technician supply and pay (Punctual Pros). Reading now: $42.03 an hour construction pay. +4.7% vs a year ago. Today: Hurts. High. What to do: Run an apprentice program, set pay bands by market, let the voice agent book calls. Size (est.): Today's +4.7% ≈ −$363K margin a year est.

Age of homes (Punctual Pros). Reading now: 56% of homes built before 1980. typical home built around 1976. Today: Helps. High. What to do: Aim replacement offers and service plans at the zips with the oldest homes. Territory. Size (est.): Each 1 in 10,000 older homes that replaces a system with Punctual Pros ≈ +$1.4M sales a year est.

Equipment prices (Punctual Pros). Reading now: 326.1 (index). +4.5% vs a year ago. Today: Hurts. Medium. What to do: Update the price book every quarter and buy ahead of announced price rises. Size (est.): Today's +4.5% ≈ −$179K margin a year if not passed on est.

Heat-pump incentives (Punctual Pros). Reading now: Federal heat-pump tax credit ended. Not available for systems installed after Dec 31, 2025. Today: Hurts. Medium. What to do: Lead every heat-pump quote with the utility rebate and a monthly payment.

Fuel for the vans (Punctual Pros). Reading now: $3.81 a gallon. +24.3% vs a year ago. Today: Hurts. Medium. What to do: Tighten routes with dispatch software and add a trip charge when fuel spikes. Size (est.): Today's +$0.74 a gallon ≈ −$87.2K margin a year est.

Sponsor-backed rivals (Punctual Pros). Reading now: 17 sponsor-backed rivals on the watch list. 3,859 heating, plumbing and electrical shops in the 15 counties. Today: Hurts. Medium. What to do: Close the top tuck-ins first and put key technicians on retention plans. Market.

Refrigerant rules (Punctual Pros). Reading now: New systems use the newer refrigerants. Units built before 2025 with the old refrigerant can still be installed (rule eased May 26, 2026). Today: Helps. Medium. What to do: Quote replacements to owners of old R-22 and R-410A systems before repair refrigerant costs more.

Heating-oil prices (Punctual Pros). Reading now: $6.11 a gallon. +70.1% vs a year ago. Today: Helps. Medium. What to do: Market heat-pump conversions to oil and propane homes before the first cold snap. Size (est.): Each 1 in 10,000 oil or propane homes that converts ≈ +$537K sales a year est.

Weather (Punctual Pros). Reading now: 4 weather alerts in the footprint. Checked when this page opened. Today: Helps. Medium. What to do: Plan surge technicians from Weather and demand on alert days. Weather and demand.

Population and income (Punctual Pros). Reading now: +2.9% population since 2020. typical household income $95.5K. Today: Helps. Low. What to do: Extend routes toward the fastest-growing counties first. Territory.

New home building (Punctual Pros). Reading now: 1,044 homes permitted in Sep 2026. 17,702 in all of 2025. Today: Steady. Low. What to do: Offer builders a first-year service agreement in the counties issuing the most permits.

05 What moves sales. Weather is one force. Home sales, pay, prices, rates, grants and elections move sales too. Weather is one force. Home sales, pay, prices, rates, grants and elections move sales too.
06 All six, ranked. Each force sized in dollars, with its assumption shown. Each lever is sized in dollars from public data, with the assumption shown.

10 CET: six add-ons, four reported in October 2026. Horton turns funded wastewater plants into work CET can prime. CET has grown to six add-ons, four of them reported in October 2026. Horton turns funded wastewater plants into work CET can prime.
11 Opportunity radar: sourced bids, capital plans and older bid lists in one ranked list, colour-coded by capability. The radar ranks every sourced bid, capital plan and award by capability, value and due date.
12 Horton cross-sell: 183 treatment plants ranked by fit, funded projects first. Every treatment plant in Connecticut, Massachusetts and Rhode Island, ranked for Horton, funded projects first.
13 New owner, new capital plan. Commercial and industrial sales become an outreach list. Each commercial sale brings a new owner with a capital plan. That is the outreach list.
14 Punctual Pros. ~1.6M housing units in Central PA and the Jersey Shore. Levers: new movers, weather, adjacent zips. Punctual Pros serves Central Pennsylvania and the Jersey Shore. The levers: new movers, weather staffing and adjacent zips.
15 Weather to calls to techs. Live alerts and forecasts become a call-pressure index and a surge-staffing number. Live alerts and forecasts become a call-pressure index and the number of extra technicians to schedule.
16 Every home sale is a lead. Scored deed records, with an offer per house and a mailing list. Every closed home sale in the footprint becomes a scored new-mover lead, with the right offer attached.
17 Tuck-ins. The Punctual Pros add-on list, led by same-brand franchisees, against the PE-backed rivals bidding for them. The Punctual Pros add-on list, led by same-brand franchisees, against the PE-backed rivals bidding for them.
18 Frontline Managed Services. 147 large law firms, most likely clients already. Growth is cross-sell: cyber, billing, an AI help desk. Frontline serves over eight hundred law firms. The account map shows where cross-sell is largest.
19 Cyber-first cross-sell. Tier-1 accounts at 5/5 cyber urgency, each with a bundle and a next action. Filter to Tier-one accounts with the highest cyber urgency; each opens a service bundle and a next action.
20 Deal math from filings. ~$137M of equity and a $90M loan imply a ~$230–260M EV. Public filings imply an enterprise value of roughly two hundred thirty to two hundred sixty million dollars.
21 Thomas Scientific. 643 Pursue accounts bill ~$3.1B of 2023 Medicare lab volume: the named-account list. Thomas Scientific: six hundred forty Pursue accounts bill about three billion dollars of Medicare lab volume.
22 Accounts: Pursue sites rolled up to parents, with a play per archetype and a CSV export. Accounts roll Pursue sites up to parents, with a selling play for each archetype.
23 Site explorer: filter to a call list by state, archetype and priority, then export it. The site explorer turns the map into a call list for the CRM.
24 Financials: COVID revenue has normalized and peers grow ~2%, so share of wallet is the lever. COVID revenue has normalized and peers barely grow, so share of wallet is the lever.
25 Bully Pulpit International. A ~400-person public-affairs firm built on 6 add-ons since April 2023. Bully Pulpit is a roughly four-hundred-person transatlantic public-affairs firm, built on six add-ons since April 2023.
26 12 sourced growth opportunities: federal comms recompetes, AI-era reputation work, litigation comms and EU corporate affairs. Twelve sourced growth plays, from federal communications recompetes to AI-era reputation advisory.
27 Valued against public-affairs deals: PPHC's ~8.4x is the floor, KKR's FGS Global deal the ceiling. BPI is valued against public-affairs deals: PPHC at about eight times EBITDA is the floor.
28 Fair Harbor. 4.5 years in. First questions: sell-through, markdowns (38.5% of variants), wholesale doors. For Fair Harbor, the first questions for management are sell-through, markdowns and wholesale doors.
29 9 sourced growth plays ranked by capital and time to revenue. Quick wins first; builds wait on sell-through. Nine sourced growth plays, ranked by capital intensity and time to revenue.
30 Filings. $30.7M of entry equity is the hard number; revenue and EBITDA are estimates. The equity check is the hard number. Revenue and EBITDA stay estimates until management shares the books.
31 Acquisition engine. Every screened add-on across the portfolio, ranked, with this quarter’s top ten. The acquisition engine ranks every screened add-on across the portfolio, with this quarter's top ten.
32 One target list. Every add-on target across six companies; pick a company for its thesis, map and ranked picks. One list holds every add-on target. Pick a company for its thesis, map and ranked picks.
33 Rival companies. Lender filings flag stressed consolidators: likely sellers, not bidders. Lender filings flag rival consolidators paying interest in kind: likely sellers, not bidders.
34 PE landscape. 35 sponsors chase the same deals; 9 are high-threat. Median rival fund: ~4.5× Fund I. Thirty-five sponsors chase the same deals, nine of them high-threat. Win on focus, not price.
35 Sector grid. Punctual Pros sits in the most crowded field; CET and Frontline still have room. Residential services is the most crowded field; CET and Frontline still have open space to accelerate add-ons.
36 Deal flow 2025–26. Every disclosed rival deal, with those in portfolio sectors flagged. Every disclosed rival deal since January 2025, with those in portfolio sectors flagged.
37 How BSP buys. Seven companies bought, twenty-one named add-ons and one exit, each with seller, advisers and lenders. Every disclosed deal: seven companies bought, twenty-one named add-ons and one exit, each with seller and lenders.
38 Deal patterns. Thesis first, founder CEOs stay, first add-on near month eight, a new lender each time. The patterns: thesis first, founder CEOs stay, first add-on near month eight, a new lender each time.
39 The rubric. Ten inferred criteria scored across every target, with the top fifteen and an intro path. The rubric scores every add-on target on ten inferred criteria. Start with the top fifteen.
40 Sponsor precedents. Thirty-four sponsor-built companies on one clock, with Punctual Pros at month thirty. Thirty-four sponsor-built companies on one clock. Punctual Pros sits at month thirty.
41 Levers. Operator team first, first add-on near month seven, then a deal every four to five months. Operator team first, the first add-on near month seven, then a deal every four to five months.
42 The Punctual Pros sequence. Three steps done, twelve recommended over 36 months. For Punctual Pros, a thirty-six month sequence: integration leader, one contact center, memberships, steady tuck-ins.
43 County scorer. All 3,144 US counties scored on eight weighted public signals. Drag a weight to re-rank. Every US county, scored on eight public signals. Change a weight and the map re-ranks.
44 Punctual Pros phases. Core, tuck-ins, Mid-Atlantic metros, then Sun Belt and Midwest franchise markets. The four Punctual Pros phases sit on the same county scores, from core to Sun Belt.
45 Top 25 metros. County scores rolled up to metro areas, with Authority Brands offices marked. County scores roll up to the top twenty-five metro areas, with the Authority Brands offices already in each.
46 Tech enablement. One operating system per company, built from proven vendors and tied to buyer KPIs. One operating system per company, built from proven vendors and tied to the KPIs buyers pay for.
47 Why buyers pay. Repeatable earnings trade at 10x+, project work at 5–6x; tech earns 0.5–2.5 turns. Repeatable earnings trade at ten times or more, project work at five to six. Tech earns part.
48 24-month roadmap. First value inside 18 months; LabOS must land before the December 2027 maturity. Every program shows value within eighteen months. LabOS must land before the December 2027 maturity.
49 Value math. Uplift times multiple, plus re-rating, minus spend: ServiceOS alone adds an est. ~$11M of EV. The calculator turns margin uplift and re-rating into value, net of spend. Every input is an estimate.
50 Portfolio financials. SEC fund filings show the capital; company financials are estimated from public records. SEC fund filings show the capital. Company financials are estimated from public records.
51 Public comparables. 31 listed peers set the margin, growth and revenue-per-employee bar for each portfolio company. Thirty-one listed peers benchmark growth, margin and revenue per employee for every portfolio company.
52 Methods and gaps. Every number has a formula and a source; each open gap names where to look next. Every number has a formula and a source, and each open gap names where to look next.
53 Monday priorities. CET: win near-term bids, cross-sell Horton · Punctual Pros: capture new movers, staff to weather. To recap: CET wins near-term bids and cross-sells Horton; Punctual Pros captures movers and staffs to weather.
54 Across the portfolio. Frontline and Thomas sell into ranked accounts; BPI and Fair Harbor chase sourced growth. Frontline and Thomas sell into ranked account lists; BPI and Fair Harbor pursue growth plays.
55 Public and licensed data · verify before use. Replay any chapter from this screen. Everything here is public or licensed research. Verify before use.

What the filings say

Home services is splitting in two.
The scaled companies (Wrench, Apex, Redwood, Legacy) borrow at SOFR + 4.25–4.75%, valued by lenders at full face value, with delayed-draw lines (credit the company draws later, as add-ons close) for acquisitions. The next tier (TurnPoint, Horizon, Any Hour, Len the Plumber) has moved to part PIK interest and is marked at 89–94. Lenders are paying for scale and punishing leverage taken on at 2021-era prices.

Punctual Pros' PA/NJ/DE footprint is exposed to the stressed side: Horizon Services (HGH Purchaser) has at least $211M…
of first lien at Blue Owl alone, paying 3.75% PIK, marked 92.5, with lenders also holding its common equity. Heartland's debt matures Dec 15, 2026. So two regional competitors are likely to sell assets or be restructured in the next 12 months rather than bid aggressively for add-ons.

Sila (King of Prussia) and Haller (Lancaster, 254 trucks) are the healthier local rivals.
Sila's 2,500+ employees imply about $0.45–0.65B revenue, versus a single ~96-person company in its 2020 PPP record, so its growth has come almost entirely from acquisitions.

For CET, IES's Commercial & Industrial segment is the cleanest margin benchmark: $427.7M revenue, 20.3% gross margin, 11.0% operating margin…
and backlog that doubled to $625.2M. Across the whole company, IES earns 11.4% operating margins with no net debt, so it can pay strategic prices for New England contractors.

PPP data puts CET's largest private MA competitors at about $100–135M (Interstate Electrical: $8.57M loan, 500 jobs…
~$41.1M payroll costs) and at least $120–160M (J&M Brown: $10M capped loan, 445 jobs, payroll costs of at least $48M). Both are family-owned union contractors with no lender filings, so they compete on labor capacity rather than on capital.

Legal services lenders are signaling real stress.
Consilio's term loan fell from 90.95 to 77.85–82.94 in the first half of 2026 with a May 2028 maturity, and Epiq's (DTI Holdco) traded at 89–93. That is consistent with AI compressing managed-review and eDiscovery revenue, and it weakens two large vendors that compete with Frontline for law-firm technology budgets.

Integreon (WhiteHorse/Twin Brook unitranche, SOFR + 5.50%, June 2027 maturity) and Kraft Kennedy (about 100 staff and ~$7.5M payroll in 2020…
implying ~$20–30M revenue) are the rivals closest to Frontline in size. Kraft Kennedy's SOC/security push matches the upsell path Frontline is pursuing with AmLaw firms.

In lab distribution, Avantor's $785M goodwill impairment on VWR…
4.6% Lab Solutions sales decline and 10.2% Q2-2026 adjusted operating margin at VWR Distribution & Services give Thomas Scientific a vulnerable category leader to take share from and a realistic margin ceiling. Calibre Scientific (SOFR + 6.00% debt maturing June 2027, CEO departed March 2026) looks like a 2026–27 refinancing or sale.

In strategic communications, KKR's $1.7B enterprise value for FGS (WPP stake $775M), financed with an SOFR + 4.50% unitranche…
sets a premium valuation. Precision Strategies' new March-2026 leverage facility (about $10.7M visible at Stellus) shows sponsors are now financing mid-size Democratic-aligned agencies like BPI.

Stagwell's Communications segment (SKDK) lost 16.5% of organic net revenue in 2025, and advocacy alone fell $62.7M.
That quantifies the election-cycle swing BPI should expect: a sharp off-year decline followed by an 11% consolidated revenue recovery in Q2 2026 heading into the midterms.

In apparel, Chubbies (Fair Harbor's closest public comparison) earned about $22.4M of segment contribution on $122.9M of FY2025…
sales (57.9% gross margin). But Q2-2026 DTC (direct-to-consumer) sales fell 20.8%, and its parent Solo Brands was delisted from the NYSE in July 2026 with about $249M of debt, so a Chubbies sale is plausible. Private Vuori and Outerknown left no SEC or PPP trace.

Financial picture
what public filings say

Scale before the deal: The Rohrer Company's April 2020 PPP loan of $745,985 implies ~$3.58M of 2019 payroll costs. At Lancaster's 2019 trade wage (~$62K) that is ~50-58 employees and roughly $9-12M of 2019 revenue (payroll at 30-40% of revenue); confidence medium.
Growth into the deal: headcount of ~113 by 2024 roughly doubles the PPP-implied base. At 2024 Lancaster wages of ~$76K and a 40-45% total labor ratio, that supports a PA revenue run-rate of ~$18-22M at the time of the BSP purchase.
FDD cross-check: the 2026 FDD franchisee lists show Punctual Pros operates 25 territories (PA: 9 One Hour, 7 Ben Franklin, 3 Mister Sparky; NJ: 3/2/1). Mapping those to Item 19 quartiles gives ~$12-19M for PA and ~$3-5M for NJ in FY2025. Blending both methods, FY2025 pro forma revenue is estimated at ~$22M (range $16-28M), about $0.9M per territory, above system averages of $0.61-0.66M per territory for One Hour and Ben Franklin.
Franchise cost: royalty (6%) plus tiered brand fund (~1.2-1.5%) takes ~7.2-7.5% of revenue (~$1.6M a year), which caps adjusted EBITDA margins at about 8-14%. Estimated adjusted EBITDA is ~$1.8-3.1M (central ~$2.6M), confidence low.
Leverage: PGIM Private Credit Fund's Jun 30, 2026 10-Q discloses a first-lien loan to Punctual Pros Midco, LLC at 3M SOFR+5.00% (8.73%), maturing Mar 26, 2029: $4.83M funded, fair value ~98.6% of par, plus a $1.4M unfunded delayed-draw (credit the company draws later, as add-ons close) commitment. This confirms a senior-secured, sponsor-style unitranche (a single term loan that blends senior and junior debt) with an acquisition line. Total facility size is not disclosed; assuming PGIM-managed accounts hold most or all of it, total senior debt is plausibly ~$10-18M (~4-5.5x EBITDA, ~$0.9-1.6M of annual cash interest), confidence low.
Entry value: the undisclosed price, a lower-middle-market sell-side advisor (Boxwood) and no dedicated co-invest SPV (unlike Thomas Scientific, Frontline and CET) all point to an enterprise value probably in the ~$18-30M range and a Fund I equity check of roughly $8-15M, about 3-4% of the $335M fund; confidence low.
Growth drivers: 2025 same-store sales grew +8.4% (One Hour), +8.9% (Ben Franklin) and +14.3% (Mister Sparky) system-wide after a soft 2024. Punctual's PA territory count was flat, so growth is organic within existing territories plus the Horvath tuck-in (PPP-implied ~$3-4M 2019 revenue, 6 territories).
Demand signal: county deed records shows ~2,100 meaningful home sales per quarter inside the 248 modeled PA territory zips (~$574M priced volume in 90 days). That is a quantifiable new-mover lead pool, where a 5% capture rate means ~425 new relationships a year.
Clean profile: no OSHA inspections were found for Punctual/Rohrer/Horvath. The HQ property is held by a separate, likely related-party real-estate LLC (assessed $914.5K, recorded $1.5M sale), so rent is a normalization item.
Overall: the public record supports a ~$20-25M-revenue, ~$2-3M-EBITDA, moderately levered (4-5x) franchise-operator portfolio company with a funded path for tuck-ins. Revenue ranges are medium confidence; EBITDA, debt and valuation are low confidence until confirmed by PitchBook or lender data.

Read-across by sector
What each benchmark implies for BSP

What this implies for Punctual Pros. Public residential/trade comps grew a median 13.6% in their latest year at a 14.4% operating margin (13.1% multi-year average), but the set is bimodal: installers IBP/BLD are flat (+1.0%/+1.5%) at 13-15% margins while FIX (+29.5%) and LMB (+24.7%) are growing on non-residential/data-center mechanical work, so residential-only demand is closer to low single digits. For Punctual Pros, a mid-teens EBITDA margin (IBP 15.1%, BLD 17.8%, FTDR 24.2% on an asset-light warranty model) is the realistic mature target, and a technician-led service model should sit near the ~$285k-$400k revenue/employee band of IBP, BLD and FIX. Growth above the ~2-4% revenue CAGR of the installers will need density-building tuck-ins and service-agreement/recurring revenue, which is the lever the portal's territory model should prioritize.
What this implies for CET. Electrical/MEP and energy contractors are in a capex upcycle: median latest-year revenue growth is 16.9% (3-yr CAGR 16.8%) led by FIX, PWR, PRIM and IESC on data-center, grid and industrial work. Margins are structurally thin, with a median operating margin of 6.4% and approximate EBITDA margin of 11.2%, and only specialist/self-perform leaders (FIX 14.4%, IESC 11.4%, EME 10.1%) clear 10%; revenue per employee clusters tightly at ~$330k-$410k (Ameresco's $1.2M reflects pass-through project costs). For CET / NuWave, that implies a benchmark of roughly $330k-$410k revenue per field+office head and a 6-10% operating margin, with upside tied to mission-critical and service/maintenance mix rather than bid-hard GC work.
What this implies for Frontline. BPO/managed-services comps posted a median 10.1% latest-year growth at a 12.6% operating margin and ~16.9% EBITDA margin, with TaskUs (+19.0%) and EXL (+13.6%) outgrowing Genpact (+6.6%) and WNS/Kyndryl flat. Revenue per employee is a delivery-model signal rather than a quality signal: offshore-heavy Genpact/EXL/TaskUs/WNS run $18k-$35k per head, while onshore professional-services models (CBIZ $290k, Kyndryl $210k) run 6-15x higher, so the revenue-per-employee benchmark for this sector uses the onshore comps only (about $250k). For Frontline, an onshore US legal-services model should be benchmarked on the CBIZ-type revenue/employee and 8-12% operating margins, with offshore leverage the main path toward Genpact/EXL-style 15% margins; CBIZ's pending $55/share cash sale to a Grant Thornton affiliate is also a live valuation marker for Smith + Howard-type accounting companies.
What this implies for Thomas Scientific. Lab and healthcare distribution is a low-growth, scale-margin business: median latest-year growth is 1.5% (3-yr CAGR 2.0%) and median operating margin 5.0% (7.4% multi-year average), with pure distributors HSIC and PDCO at ~4-5% while manufacturer-distributors TMO and TECH earn 17-21%. Revenue per employee for distributors runs roughly $485k-$865k (AVTR $485k, HSIC $527k, PDCO $864k), well above service businesses because product pass-through dominates revenue. For Thomas Scientific, a 4-7% EBITDA-to-revenue profile with $500k+ revenue per employee is the distribution benchmark, and margin expansion must come from proprietary/private-label mix and account penetration, since end-market volume growth is running near flat.
Holding-company read-across. Agency holding companies are shrinking or flat on a like-for-like basis: median latest-year growth is 0.3%, with WPP down 8.1% in GBP, IPG down 1.8% before its sale, Stagwell +2.4%, and Omnicom's +10.1% driven by the IPG acquisition. Reported margins are distorted by impairments and deal costs (median latest operating margin 4.2% vs a 7.8% multi-year average), while normalized holding-company margins sit around 11-15% (OMC and IPG before 2025) and revenue per employee is ~$145k-$265k. For a BSP agency portfolio company, benchmarks are roughly $190k-$265k revenue per employee and a 10-15% EBITDA margin, and growth has to come from specialist/earned-media and data capabilities because the category itself is ex-growth and consolidating.
What this implies for Fair Harbor. Apparel/DTC (direct-to-consumer) comps are bifurcated: the median latest-year growth is -1.5% and median operating margin 3.7%, but LULU (19.9%) and CROX (about 25-26% in FY2023-24, before its 2025 impairments) show what brand heat earns, while DLTH, RVLV and BIRD run -2% to 6% or deep losses. Allbirds (revenue down 19.7%, -52% operating margin, headcount 927 to 362 in two years) is the cautionary case for a single-category, DTC-first, sustainability-positioned footwear/apparel brand scaling stores too early. For Fair Harbor, the benchmark is roughly $275k-$500k revenue per employee and a positive high-single-digit EBITDA margin before scaling retail, with wholesale/marketplace mix (as Crocs and Revolve show) preferable to heavy owned-store build-outs.

Implications for BSP
Research read-across of the comparables

31 public peers split the BSP portfolio into three economic regimes.
(1) Construction and trades (CET, Punctual Pros) lead growth: electrical/MEP comps compounded revenue at 16.8% a year (FY2023-25), versus 8.4% for residential. The trades still have thin margins, with a median operating margin of 6.4% for commercial electrical, 11.2% approximate EBITDA, and only specialists like FIX (14.4%), IESC (11.4%) and EME (10.1%) at or above 10%, so contractor value creation comes from mix (service, mission-critical) more than price. Residential comps show the split Punctual Pros faces: pure residential installers IBP and TopBuild grew only 1-1.5% in FY2025 at 13-15% operating margins, while the fast growers (FIX, LMB) are leaning on non-residential work. Frontdoor's 24% approximate EBITDA margin on about $1.03M revenue per employee shows the value of a subscription and asset-light contractor-network model in home services.
(2) Services and people businesses (Frontline, the agency holding) are priced on productivity per head. Offshore BPO earns 12-15% operating margins at only $18k-$35k revenue per employee, while onshore professional services (CBIZ $290k, Kyndryl $210k) earn 3-9%. So a US-heavy legal or accounting company should expect CBIZ-like economics unless it adds offshore leverage. Agencies are ex-growth (median +0.3%, WPP -8.1% in GBP) and consolidating (Omnicom absorbed Interpublic, taking headcount from 74,900 to about 120,000), so a BSP agency asset has to win on specialist growth rather than category tailwind.
(3) Product businesses (Thomas Scientific, Fair Harbor) are scale-and-mix stories. Lab distribution grows at a median 1.5% with 4-5% operating margins for pure distributors (HSIC, PDCO), against 17-21% for manufacturers (TMO, TECH), so private-label and proprietary content are the margin lever for Thomas Scientific. Apparel/DTC is the most dispersed sector: LULU earns about 20% operating margin, but Duluth and Allbirds show negative margins and shrinking revenue, and Allbirds went from 927 to 362 employees in two years. For Fair Harbor, capital discipline around retail expansion matters more than top-line speed. Finally, M&A activity among the comps (QXO/TopBuild, the WNS and Patterson take-outs in 2025, Omnicom/Interpublic, Grant Thornton affiliate/CBIZ at $55 cash, Merck KGaA/Bio-Techne) signals active strategic and sponsor demand in four of BSP's six sectors, which supports exit optionality for the portfolio.

What moves sales at CET: the market, cost, labor, calendar and weather forces, why each matters, today's reading and the move.

11 forces, 4 hurting, 2 helping. Revenue $82.5M est.

Public project money (CET). Reading now: $76.6M federal electrical and HVAC contracts. fiscal 2026, −40.3% vs the year before. Today: Hurts. High. What to do: Work funded projects on the bid radar; state water and school money now beats federal awards. Opportunity radar.

Copper and electrical gear (CET). Reading now: $14,473 a ton. +44.8% vs a year ago. Today: Hurts. High. What to do: Add price-escalation clauses to bids and order long-lead gear at award. Size (est.): Today's +44.8% ≈ −$1.5M margin a year est.

Electrician supply and pay (CET). Reading now: 298K openings in construction. +44.7% vs a year ago. Today: Hurts. High. What to do: Grow the apprentice pipeline and share crews across Horton and CET. Size (est.): Today's +4.7% ≈ −$1.6M margin a year est.

Wastewater compliance (CET). Reading now: 52 large treatment plants with open violations. of 175 large plants in CT, MA and RI. Today: Helps. High. What to do: Pitch Horton pump-station, power and controls work to the plants with open violations. Wastewater accounts.

Commercial and public building (CET). Reading now: $1.32T a year. +1.8% vs a year ago. Today: Steady. High. What to do: Keep the bid calendar full in the sectors still building: water, schools and health care. Opportunity radar. Size (est.): Today's +1.8% ≈ +$891K sales a year est.

Solar and charger credits (CET). Reading now: Charger credit has ended; solar credit closes after 2027. Solar projects not started by Jul 4, 2026 must be running by Dec 31, 2027. Today: Hurts. Medium. What to do: Finish projects that still qualify; steer new sales to storage, efficiency and wastewater work.

Utility efficiency programs (CET). Reading now: Mass Save and Energize CT plans run through 2027. Rebates for lighting, controls and heat pumps. Today: Helps. Medium. What to do: Keep NuWave a top program vendor and fold rebates into every quote.

Power prices (CET). Reading now: 19.0¢ a kWh. +1.1% vs a year ago. Today: Steady. Medium. What to do: Open each proposal with the payback at today’s power price.

Borrowing costs (CET). Reading now: 7.00%. +0.00 pts vs a year ago. Today: Steady. Medium. What to do: Bring lease and pay-from-savings partners into large proposals.

Property changing hands (CET). Reading now: 9,060 new home listings. −1.0% vs a year ago. Today: Steady. Low. What to do: Reach new owners through the Property transfers list. Property transfers.

Weather (CET). Reading now: No weather alerts in operating counties. Checked when this page opened. Today: Steady. Low. What to do: Keep an on-call crew for pump-station and generator outages.

Thesis analyst view

Punctual Pros has 103 residential HVAC, plumbing and electrical operators screened across PA, NJ, MD and DE (PA 48, NJ 37, MD 10, NY 5, DE 3). 36 are density tuck-ins (≤30 mi straight-line (≈45 drive-min) of Lancaster, Harrisburg, York or Toms River) that add route density to existing dispatch; the other 66 are new-hub anchors, i.e. branch acquisitions that need their own GM, dispatch and marketing plan. 1 more trades under the Punctual Pros name and is held out until affiliation is confirmed. 16 already run all three trades, 11 operate Authority Brands territories that could transfer, and 10 have 1,000+ reviews. text:
What Broad Sky OS knows about home sales: the home-sales data the portal holds for the territory of Punctual Pros, a Broad Sky Partners (BSP) company.

Coverage. The home-sales records hold public recorded sales for four New Jersey counties (Atlantic, Burlington, Monmouth and Ocean) and eleven Pennsylvania counties (Adams, Berks, Chester, Cumberland, Dauphin, Franklin, Lancaster, Lebanon, Montgomery, Perry and York). Each record is one recorded sale: the address, town, ZIP code, sale date and price, and the year built, size and bedrooms where the county publishes them.

Sources. All public. New Jersey comes from the Division of Taxation's statewide sales file. Pennsylvania comes from each county's open parcel or assessment data.

How current. Public sale records run behind, so recorded sales are never this month's sales. New Jersey sales reach Oct 15, 2026; the newest full month is July 2026. Pennsylvania sales reach Nov 10, 2026; the newest full month is September 2026. The records were last pulled on Nov 16, 2026.

New Jersey home sales by county: the date sales reach and the newest full month.
Atlantic County, NJ: sales reach Sep 30, 2026; newest full month July 2026.
Burlington County, NJ: sales reach Sep 25, 2026; newest full month July 2026.
Monmouth County, NJ: sales reach Oct 9, 2026; newest full month August 2026.
Ocean County, NJ: sales reach Oct 15, 2026; newest full month August 2026.

Pennsylvania home sales by county: the date sales reach and the newest full month.
Adams County, PA: sales reach Oct 23, 2026; newest full month August 2026.
Berks County, PA: sales reach Oct 20, 2026; newest full month September 2026.
Chester County, PA: sales reach Oct 15, 2026; newest full month September 2026.
Cumberland County, PA: sales reach Oct 21, 2026; newest full month September 2026.
Dauphin County, PA: sales reach Jun 30, 2026; no full recent month.
Franklin County, PA: sales reach Dec 17, 2025; no full recent month.
Lancaster County, PA: sales reach Nov 10, 2026; newest full month October 2026.
Lebanon County, PA: sales reach Nov 4, 2026; newest full month October 2026.
Montgomery County, PA: sales reach Nov 3, 2026; newest full month September 2026.
Perry County, PA: sales reach Oct 2, 2026; newest full month August 2026.
York County, PA: sales reach Nov 6, 2026; newest full month September 2026.

Gaps. Dauphin County is frozen: a partial snapshot taken Sep 24, 2026. The county site does not allow automated access, so its records do not get newer and do not show the county's real sales volume. Franklin County is thin: the county's public file stops at Dec 17, 2025, so it has no full recent month.

What the assistant can do with them. A new-homeowner list: recent home buyers by county, town or ZIP code, ranked for the new-homeowner promotion. An address brief: what the public record says about one address, what to check on arrival and which offers are worth raising. For a New Jersey address the brief also checks the state parcel and tax list and the construction permit data. Pennsylvania has no public permit feed, so a Pennsylvania brief uses the sale record only.

No owner names. Buyer and seller names are not stored, so no list and no brief names an owner. Mail is addressed to "New homeowner".

Limits. Every list and brief states the date the sales reach and the date the records were pulled. A purchase after that date is not in the records yet.

text:
Agents by company with triggers, annual value and time to deploy

Generated: 2026-10-06
Method: Agents were designed per portfolio company from each OS's systems of record and existing portal sources (ServiceOS evidence, CET opportunity radar, CET wastewater-plant targets, Punctual Pros storm-event history, Punctual Pros demand model, BPI filings, filings sources estimate tables). Each agent cites one sourced metric (vendor case study, benchmark, regulator or academic study) found by web search and direct fetch on 2026-10-06. estimated annual value is an explicit analyst assumption computed from the formula in estimated-annual-value formula, with vendor claims haircut (typically by half) and run-costs netted where material; it is EBITDA-equivalent run-rate after ramp, not a forecast. Revenue bases are the midpoints of low-confidence portal estimates: PP ~$22M, CET+Horton+NuWave ~$80M, Frontline ~$120M, Thomas ~$285M, BPI ~$105M net, Fair Harbor ~$27.5M.
Caveats:
- All estimated annual value figures are assumptions, not company data; volumes (calls, tickets, invoices, quotes, members) are analyst estimates and must be replaced with system-of-record counts.
- Most metric claim figures come from vendor case studies (Avoca, ServiceTitan, Rilla, Togal.AI, Vic.ai, Conexiom, HighRadius, Proton.ai, Gorgias, Loopio, Rewst, Intapp); they are self-selected and unaudited, so values apply roughly 50% haircuts.
- Value lines overlap in places (e.g., PP dispatch and surge agents both lift booked revenue; TS quote and cross-sell agents share the same customers); the total is a ceiling until de-duplicated against measured baselines.
- MetricNet cost-per-ticket figures date from 2011 and are directional; Frontline's ticket volume is assumed from its stated ~250,000 supported users.
- AI rules are changing quickly; the operating controls on this page are designed to hold regardless.
- Some vendor availability (e.g., Procore Helix agents in limited release) and pricing may have changed; confirm in pilots.
- CET agents start with the six New England states, where the bid data is. Smith + Howard is exited and excluded.
- Gartner forecasts over 40% of agentic AI projects will be canceled by end-2027; the kill criteria in gov-09 are part of the plan, not an afterthought.
Program summary: 45 AI agents cover BSP's six active companies, one set per operating system (ServiceOS, GridOS, FirmOS, LabOS, SignalOS, HarborOS), built from 8 reusable patterns. Each agent starts on an event, such as a missed call, an NWS alert, a deed record, a bid posting or an invoice, so no one has to remember to start it. Every agent also names the person who approves its consequential actions; no agent moves money, prices below a margin floor, posts publicly or disables an account on its own. On labelled analyst assumptions the program is worth about $12.7M a year of run-rate EBITDA-equivalent value once ramped, led by Thomas Scientific ($3.8M) and Frontline ($3.6M). Punctual Pros ($0.9M) gets the most agents per dollar of revenue because missed calls, dispatch, options, memberships and permits are where home-services margin is won or lost. CET ($1.3M) uses agents to pick better bids, estimate faster and turn NuWave and EV monitoring into recurring revenue. BPI ($2.3M) and Fair Harbor ($0.8M) use agents to productize monitoring, protect client confidentiality while drafting faster, and cut returns and excess inventory. Rollout runs in four waves over 18 months, starting with inbound-contact and document agents that have the clearest baselines and lowest risk, then finance, then revenue agents, then monitoring services. Portfolio Resource Group (PRG) governance sets least-privilege access, consequence-based approval tiers, full audit logs, approved model terms with no training on portfolio data, vendor AI reviews, and kill criteria tied to measured value. Values are estimates built from vendor case studies and public benchmarks with explicit haircuts; each must be re-based on the company's own 8-week baseline before it is counted in an exit narrative like Smith + Howard's.

Caveats:
- FEC disbursements are gross billings to BPI, mostly pass-through media spend; they are not BPI revenue. The by-recipient aggregation may include memo or duplicate entries and only covers federal committees; state and local committees, 501(c)(4)s and corporate advocacy clients are not captured.

(2) A senior secured Credit and Guaranty Agreement followed on 7 Dec 2023, with PineBridge Private Credit Agent LLC as administrative agent and Alter Domus as collateral agent. It was amended on 29 Oct 2024, the day the UK add-ons closed, and the UK subsidiaries granted all-asset debentures in Jan 2025. So the facility funds M&A, and debt has probably grown with each tuck-in. (3) Scale is best measured by headcount: more than 250 staff in Dec 2023 (after BOLDT), more than 325 in Nov 2024 and more than 350 in Mar 2025, across 14 offices in 6 countries. Adding Agado (May 2025) and 365 Sherpas (May 2026), we estimate about 375-425 people today. (4) Applying public-affairs and PR net revenue per head of about $240-340K gives 2025 net (fee) revenue of roughly $85-125M, while gross billings including pass-through media are materially higher. (5) The PPP record ($2.221M approved Apr 2020, cancelled 5 May 2020) implies about $10.7M of capped payroll and roughly 100-150 staff in early 2020, so the company has roughly tripled in five years, about half through acquisitions. (6) Political work is large but cyclical: federal committees paid BPI $115.3M in the 2024 cycle, including $114.2M from the Biden/Harris committee, and $96.5M in 2020, against only $3.1M in 2022 and $41K so far in 2026. 2024 was therefore a peak year and 2025 an off-year trough, a pattern Stagwell confirms with a $62.7M off-year advocacy decline and a 28.5% segment EBITDA drop in 2025. (7) Listed peers bound margins: PPHC earns a 24-26% adjusted EBITDA margin and Stagwell Communications 26-33% of net revenue. For a media-heavy BPI we assume 18-24% of net revenue, or about $17-28M of 2025 EBITDA, with 2024 likely higher. (8) With typical lower-middle-market leverage of 3.5-5.0x, senior debt is likely about $60-110M, but the principal is not disclosed anywhere public. (9) Sponsor equity of $90M suggests an entry enterprise value of about $150-220M, depending on whether acquisition debt was in place at close (the credit agreement post-dates the close by 7 months), or about 10-13x an estimated $14-18M of 2022-23 EBITDA. (10) UK entities give hard data points: Seven Hills has about 40 staff, retained about £0.85M of FY2025 earnings and held £1.73M cash; Message House had 16 staff, £1.80M cash and £3.04M net assets. That supports an estimate of UK annual revenue in the low-to-mid-teens of millions of pounds across about 70 London staff. (11) Overall, BPI looks like a roughly $100M-plus fee-revenue, roughly $20-25M EBITDA agency that has diversified from US Democratic political media into corporate affairs and Europe. It will likely be marketed around the 2027-28 cycle to strategics (e.g. Stagwell, PPHC, FGS, Teneo) or a larger sponsor.

text:
Phases, levers, AI agents and the roadmap for BPI

Title: Bully Pulpit International: the growth plan
Subject: Bully Pulpit International (BPI), a BSP portfolio company since 2023-04-27
Generated: 2026-10-06
Thesis: From agency to productized communications company: AI-era reputation work, public affairs for regulated sectors (energy, AI, health), European add-ons and retainers over projects. Add-ons are specialist shops; AI agents handle monitoring, compliant drafting and audience testing.
Method: Built on 2026-10-06 from the repo sources BPI filings (estimate table, FEC/Companies House/Form D items), BSP firm profile (bsp-bpi add-ons, timeline, BPI opportunities), public comparables (communications agencies benchmarks), PE landscape (sponsors overlapping BPI), ServiceOS evidence (ra-bpi, kb-bpi-*, ve-20..23, vs-bpi-*) and rival filings (FGS, Precision Strategies, Stagwell). Added web research fetched 2026-10-06: BSP Smith + Howard exit release, Canaccord/O'Dwyer's/PrivSource for Penta, Wikipedia/WPP 6-K for FGS, CVC for Teneo, BPI releases, Forrester TEI pages (Writer, Quid, Microsoft), EY/Aaru, Muck Rack via GlobeNewswire, Quorum, Davis+Gilbert 2025 PDF (text-extracted) and the IPA Agency Census 2025. Expansion-phase data points are computed in code from the repo sources (cadences, ratios, sums of opportunity ceilings). KPI targets and KPI roadmap are explicit analyst assumptions anchored to the BPI filings midpoints.
Caveats:
- BPI revenue, EBITDA, headcount and debt are low-confidence analyst estimates from BPI filings, not company disclosures. Every KPI target and KPI roadmap figure is an assumption (label est.).
- FEC figures are gross political billings, mostly pass-through media, not BPI revenue. The 2022 figure ($3.1M) comes from the BPI filings financial picture because the item-level cycle series was removed in verification.
- Penta revenue ($100M+, about half from AI/data) is per Axios (Aug 2025), captured from a search-result extract. Axios returned HTTP 403 on direct fetch, and the O'Dwyer's and Canaccord pages confirm the deal but not revenue.
- Teneo ~$700M valuation comes from press summaries (PRovoke/Holmes Report via search). The CVC release confirms 800+ staff, 19 offices and 9 acquisitions since 2015 but not the price.
- AI-agent metrics are vendor-commissioned (Forrester TEI for Writer, Quid, Microsoft) or vendor case studies (Aaru/EY, Quorum). They are self-selected upper bounds. The Writer study also shows clients cutting agency scope by 50%, a substitution risk for BPI.
- Federal opportunity total ($250M) sums ceilings/values as parsed from BPI opportunities and is dominated by the NASA recompete ($202.6M base plus all options). Eligibility and set-aside status are unverified.
- International revenue share (~15-20% today) is an analyst estimate from UK Companies House staff counts and an assumed GBP/USD of 1.27. Germany and Nordics revenue is not public.
- pp_nationwide.json (the named structural template) was not present in the repo at build time, so field conventions follow assets/chat.js expansionPlan. talent program replaces pro program and phases carry KPI targets with headcount/locations instead of technicians/territories.
- Smith + Howard and BPI add-on cadences are computed from first-close/announcement dates and count Seven Hills and Message House as two add-ons.
Item counts:
Template: 18
Expansion phase: 4
Growth lever: 10
Ai agent: 9
Talent program: 6
Financing: 6
Narrative: Six add-ons since April 2023 (about 2.0 a year versus Smith + Howard's 2.4) show BPI already running the Smith + Howard plan across the Atlantic, with London its #2 hub and Germany its #3 market. Smith + Howard grew from about 100 people in one Atlanta office to about 800 in 11 locations, with 9 add-ons and nearly 4x revenue, then sold to TPG Growth in August 2026. BPI's version starts from a larger base: an estimated $85-125M of net revenue, roughly $17-28M of adjusted EBITDA and about 400 people; those are low-confidence estimates from filings, not company figures. The biggest value gap is cyclicality; federal political billings swung from $3.1M in 2022 to $115.3M in 2024, and Stagwell's comparable segment fell 16.5% organically in the year after the election. So phase one productizes the core; SignalOS packages narrative monitoring, synthetic message testing and outcome dashboards into always-on retainers, sold first through the 2026 Reputation Resilience Index briefings, where 81% of adults say AI makes false rumors too easy to spread. Phase two builds named practices where regulation guarantees recurring work (AI and tech policy, energy and critical minerals, health in Boston, and litigation and oversight), plus a federal capture team for about $250M of tracked agency communications recompetes where BPI has no prime awards today. Phase three is the transatlantic version of regional-to-national; one retainer should cover Washington, Brussels, Berlin and London, built with 2-3 specialist tuck-ins a year funded under the existing PineBridge facility, whose UK collateral package is already in place. The analogs show the exit path; Penta was built from a data asset, added Hume Brophy in Europe and sold to Shamrock in 2025 with reportedly half of its $100M+ revenue from AI and data; FGS fused US public affairs with UK and German corporate affairs and reached a $1.7B enterprise value with KKR. The AI agents we would deploy first are a narrative early-warning monitor, a compliance-gated drafting agent and a synthetic-audience tester; each is backed by vendor evidence such as 85% faster review cycles (Writer) and a 0.90 survey correlation in one day (Aaru for EY), which we treat as upper bounds. Talent is the moat; the senior bench of LaBolt, Gibbs, Alexander and Whiting, partner equity on the FGS model, founder-to-practice-leader paths for acquired firms, and compensation held under 60% of net revenue are what keep the people the revenue walks out with. Our assumption-based roadmap takes revenue from about $105M to about $160M and EBITDA from about $22M to about $38M over 36 months, with headcount from about 400 to about 560 and recurring revenue at about 55%. At the 10-13x sponsor-exit range we estimate (PPHC trades at about 8.4x as the public floor), that implies roughly $384-499M of enterprise value after the 2028 cycle; that is an analyst scenario to pressure-test, not a forecast.
Narrative sentences:
- Six add-ons since April 2023 (about 2.0 a year versus Smith + Howard's 2.4) show BPI already running the Smith + Howard plan across the Atlantic, with London its #2 hub and Germany its #3 market.
- Smith + Howard grew from about 100 people in one Atlanta office to about 800 in 11 locations, with 9 add-ons and nearly 4x revenue, then sold to TPG Growth in August 2026.
- BPI's version starts from a larger base: an estimated $85-125M of net revenue, roughly $17-28M of adjusted EBITDA and about 400 people; those are low-confidence estimates from filings, not company figures.
- The biggest value gap is cyclicality; federal political billings swung from $3.1M in 2022 to $115.3M in 2024, and Stagwell's comparable segment fell 16.5% organically in the year after the election.
- So phase one productizes the core; SignalOS packages narrative monitoring, synthetic message testing and outcome dashboards into always-on retainers, sold first through the 2026 Reputation Resilience Index briefings, where 81% of adults say AI makes false rumors too easy to spread.
- Phase two builds named practices where regulation guarantees recurring work (AI and tech policy, energy and critical minerals, health in Boston, and litigation and oversight), plus a federal capture team for about $250M of tracked agency communications recompetes where BPI has no prime awards today.
- Phase three is the transatlantic version of regional-to-national; one retainer should cover Washington, Brussels, Berlin and London, built with 2-3 specialist tuck-ins a year funded under the existing PineBridge facility, whose UK collateral package is already in place.
- The analogs show the exit path; Penta was built from a data asset, added Hume Brophy in Europe and sold to Shamrock in 2025 with reportedly half of its $100M+ revenue from AI and data; FGS fused US public affairs with UK and German corporate affairs and reached a $1.7B enterprise value with KKR.
- The AI agents we would deploy first are a narrative early-warning monitor, a compliance-gated drafting agent and a synthetic-audience tester; each is backed by vendor evidence such as 85% faster review cycles (Writer) and a 0.90 survey correlation in one day (Aaru for EY), which we treat as upper bounds.
- Talent is the moat; the senior bench of LaBolt, Gibbs, Alexander and Whiting, partner equity on the FGS model, founder-to-practice-leader paths for acquired firms, and compensation held under 60% of net revenue are what keep the people the revenue walks out with.
- Our assumption-based roadmap takes revenue from about $105M to about $160M and EBITDA from about $22M to about $38M over 36 months, with headcount from about 400 to about 560 and recurring revenue at about 55%.
- At the 10-13x sponsor-exit range we estimate (PPHC trades at about 8.4x as the public floor), that implies roughly $384-499M of enterprise value after the 2028 cycle; that is an analyst scenario to pressure-test, not a forecast.

Pattern: Two seller archetypes, roughly half each. Sponsor-to-sponsor secondaries are the larger checks: Thomas from Carlyle, BPI from Svoboda, Frontline from BV. First-institutional-capital deals are the smaller ones: Fair Harbor (founders), Smith + Howard (first external investor), Punctual Pros (founder franchisee), CET (private owners). In 2 of 3 secondaries the prior sponsor rolled and stayed (Svoboda, BV).
Evidence deal ids:
deal-ts; deal-bpi; deal-fl; deal-fh; deal-sh; deal-pp; deal-cet
Strength: strong
Implication for next deals: For a larger company ($15M+ EBITDA), expect a sponsor seller and offer the outgoing sponsor a minority roll. For smaller companies, target founder or partner owners taking their first institutional capital.

Pattern: Founder CEOs stay; CEOs inherited from a prior sponsor get replaced at about 13-15 months. Retained: Danehy (Fair Harbor), Taylor (S+H, through exit), Bleeker (BPI), Buckwalter (Punctual Pros), Duquette (CET). Replaced: Simmons became Haas at Thomas (Apr 2023, ~15 months); Naidoo became Britt at Frontline (Jan 2026, ~13.5 months). Each outgoing CEO moved to the board, and Simmons joined BSP's Executive Board.

deal-fh; deal-sh; deal-bpi; deal-pp; deal-cet; deal-ts; deal-fl
Strength: strong
Implication for next deals: For a secondary, underwrite a CEO-succession option (an operator from the Executive Board or the network) by month 12. For a founder deal, the founder's willingness to stay 3-5 years and run M&A is a gating item.

Strength: moderate
Implication for next deals: Against a $335M Fund I, any company needing more than ~$40M of equity probably needs a co-invest SPV. Pre-sound co-invest LPs, including Carlyle AlpInvest (Frontline), when sizing the next company.

title: How BSP buys: records

text:
Kind: pattern
Pattern: The one exit follows a clear sequence: a regional founder-led firm, 9 add-ons over 3.7 years, investment in tech, AI and an India delivery center, then a sale to a larger growth-equity sponsor (TPG Growth) run by William Blair and Baird. Headcount went from ~100 to ~800 and revenue grew nearly 4x.
Evidence deal ids:
deal-sh; deal-sh-exit; deal-sh-msp; deal-sh-fahrenheit; deal-sh-geels
Strength: moderate
Implication for next deals: Plan exits around a 3.5-4.5 year hold and a sponsor buyer. A visible tech/AI and offshore-delivery story was part of TPG's quoted rationale. By hold length and add-on count, BPI (3.4 years, 6 add-ons) looks closest to exit-ready.
Source urls:
https://broadskypartners.com/broad-sky-partners-completes-sale-of-smith-howard-to-tpg/; https://www.smith-howard.com/smith-howard-announces-significant-investment-from-tpg/
Source url: https://broadskypartners.com/broad-sky-partners-completes-sale-of-smith-howard-to-tpg/
Retrieved: 2026-10-06

Kind: pattern
Pattern: Connections run through Carlyle and MidOcean. The seller and management of Thomas knew BSP's partners from their Carlyle roles. Carlyle AlpInvest co-invested $12.5M directly in Frontline. Zachem, Glucksman, Kiser, Narain and RJ David are Carlyle alumni, and Jodi Kahn was a Carlyle operating advisor. Zachem (14 years) and Marlow came from MidOcean, whose theme-driven, operating-partner model and franchise-services focus BSP mirrors. Guggenheim sold Frontline to BSP and later advised TPG on buying S+H; Baird advised Carlyle on Thomas and co-advised the S+H sale.
Evidence deal ids:
deal-ts; deal-fl; deal-sh-exit
Strength: strong
Implication for next deals: Look first at assets held by Carlyle and MidOcean-adjacent sponsors and by BV- or Svoboda-style lower-middle-market sponsors. Treat Guggenheim and Baird as two-way counterparties (they sell to BSP and buy from BSP).

Kind: pattern
Pattern: After the first deal, check sizes moved down market. Thomas used ~$236M of equity at close (with co-invest); its loan matures in December 2027. Later checks were smaller: Fair Harbor $30.7M, BPI $90M, Punctual Pros an estimated $8-15M, CET an estimated $25-45M. The exception is Frontline at $137M+$30M, a high-recurring-revenue asset.
Evidence deal ids:
deal-ts; deal-fh; deal-bpi; deal-pp; deal-cet; deal-fl
Strength: moderate
Implication for next deals: Default entry is a $2-20M EBITDA portfolio company at a sub-$100M EV, built up by add-ons. Go large only with >85% recurring revenue (Frontline-type) and avoid peak-cycle earnings (Thomas's COVID-testing bump).

Pattern: 'People-first' and culture language is used as a screening filter and as a closing tool, alongside seller equity rollover. BSP's own quotes cite 'people-first culture' at BPI and Punctual Pros. Founders roll into the company (365 Sherpas sellers become BPI shareholders; Svoboda and BV roll). S+H and add-on sellers repeatedly say culture fit decided the deal.

deal-bpi; deal-pp; deal-bpi-365sherpas; deal-fl; deal-sh-msp; deal-sh-fahrenheit; deal-sh-skc
Strength: moderate
Implication for next deals: Offer founders of add-ons rollover into the portfolio company, not only cash, and test culture fit before price. In professional services, rollover is the retention mechanism.

Kind: criterion
Criterion: Sector essentiality (non-discretionary demand)
Weight (%): 15
Test: Share of revenue tied to repair, replace, compliance, regulated or mission-critical outsourced work. Measure from service-line mix on the website, NAICS code and customer type, and for residential services the repair-vs-install mix and Google review volume.
Scoring bands:
5: >80% non-discretionary (repair, compliance, managed services)
3: 50-80%
1: <50% or discretionary consumer product

Kind: criterion
Criterion: Downside protection: earnings quality, cyclicality and leverage
Weight (%): 8
Test: Normalize for one-off peaks (Thomas COVID testing: federal revenue fell from $84-91M to $7-8M a year; BPI election-cycle billings). Leverage <=5x at entry with a DDTL for add-ons. Customer concentration <10%. Watch BDC marks after close.

5: Stable earnings, <=4.5x leverage, low concentration
3: Some cyclicality
1: Peak-cycle earnings or >6x
